https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/politics/l.text:
One year ago today Tory wrecking ball Liz Truss took up her post as PM after being trusted by tens of thousands of Conservatives to lead the country forward.
As we now know, it would all end in tears just 49 days later - making Ms Truss the shortest-serving PM in history, falling well short of the 119 days clocked up by George Canning. But at least poor Mr Canning has the excuse of having died in office way back in 1827.
It had all looked so promising for the Tory tax-cutting brigade after Ms Truss breezed into No10 when her lofty promises convinced 56% of Tory members that she was the right fit to succeed Boris Johnson. Sadly for them Ms Truss, the 56th British Prime Minister, was driven out following the chaos caused by her disastrous mini-budget.
Her tenure may have been short, but it definitely wasn't lacking in drama. During her flash-in-the pan time at the top she was described as a "libertarian jihadist" by one of her own MPs, while another lamented the lack of talent in cabinet and the Conservatives endured their most chaotic conference in a generation.
Here we look at some of the key moments of Ms Truss's premiership as millions of Brits continue to struggle with the effects of the mayhem she unleashed.
When Ms Truss was named as the 56th British Prime Minister on September 5, Tory colleagues were delighted that an ugly summer could be consigned to history. After six weeks of ugly blue-on-blue attacks, the former Foreign Secretary's victory over Rishi Sunak was confirmed after she secured the votes of 81,000 Tory members - 56% of those polled.
The following morning she travelled to Balmoral to be formally appointed by the Queen in what turned out to be the monarch's final public act. Standing outside 10 Downing Street during a brief gap between downpours hours later, Ms Truss bragged she had a "bold plan" to grow the economy.
She had a daunting task ahead of her, with soaring energy prices sparking alarm, and economists already worried about the tax cut plans she teased in her leadership campaign.
Ms Truss's first act was to purge the cabinet of those who didn't back her - a move that would backfire in the coming weeks as her popularity plummeted. After a stalled summer as the energy bills crisis worsened, she finally addressed the Commons on September 8, outlining plans to freeze bills at an average of £2,500 for two years.
Alarm bells were already ringing about how she would fund this, but minutes after her address news broke that the Queen was seriously ill - and at 6.30pm her death was confirmed by Buckingham Palace. Ten days of public mourning followed, during which world leaders descended on London for a state funeral which saw Ms Truss deliver an awkward reading derided as wooden by viewers. She admitted that she lacks flair, but vowed her plans for the economy would turn the country around.
Ms Truss's economic plans came unstuck quickly, with the botched mini-Budget - delivered by her close friend and Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng on September 23 - unleashing market chaos and sending the pound plummeting to record lows. The decision to scrap the income tax rate for the UK's highest earners and an end to a cap on bankers' bonuses particularly sparked a backlash from the public and backbenchers alike.
Nevertheless Ms Truss steadfastly stood by her actions, claiming that she had an "iron grip" on public finances and resisting calls for her to scrap the measures. "Not everyone will like what we are doing, but I want to reassure the public that the government has a clear plan that I believe is right for the country," she said.
The markets were not convinced, and the Bank of England was forced to pledge up to £65 billion to buy government gilts in order to save pension funds on the brink of collapse. Meanwhile lenders withdrew mortgage offers as interest rates soared, piling misery on already-struggling Brits.
If any evidence were needed that things were going badly, deep splits were shown up at the Conservative Party Conference in Birmingham, with questions already starting to be asked about whether Ms Truss - and the party - could weather the storm. The event had barely got going when Grant Shapps, who Ms Truss sacked as Transport Minister on her first day, branded the budget "tin-eared". Within weeks he'd hold one of the great offices of state - more on that below.
Meanwhile other heavyweights including Michael Gove and even right-winger Esther McVey hit out. The former, now safely back in the cabinet after Mr Sunak took over, said the 45p income tax cut for the rich was a “display of the wrong values".
Ms Truss had an eventful final day, taking the stage to deliver her keynote speech to M People's Movin On Up - only for one group member to spectacularly torpedo her while she was still onstage. Mike Pickering immediately lashed out at her for using their hit single, saying he did not want it to be a "soundtrack to lies". And things got awkward when Greenpeace protesters interrupted her and held up a banner asking "Who Voted For This?"
After defending the decision to cut the top tax rate from 45p to 40p, telling the BBC she would "stay the course", the PM and Mr Kwarteng were forced into a humiliating U-turn within hours. Incredibly she did a series of interviews defending her budget - but scrapped the policy in the gap before they were broadcast.
Despite alarm over a 20-year borrowing high, Ms Truss said on October 12 that she would not be reversing any more measures. Two days later, after a fraught meeting with backbenchers, she changed her tune.
Mr Kwarteng was summoned back from meetings with world finance bosses in Washington and unceremoniously sacked, having said the night before: "I'm not going anywhere." Mr Kwarteng said he had accepted the PM's request to "stand aside" as Chancellor in his resignation letter.
It was a desperate attempt to pass the buck, and she might initially have thought it was enough to keep her in a job. Jeremy Hunt was named as his successor, and seemingly given free reign to completely redraw the finance plans.
Ms Truss faced reporters in an excruciating nine-minute press conference on October 14, admitting that things weren't going as well as she'd hope. Nevertheless she refused to say sorry, and rushed out of the room as journalists hurled questions at her.
The Tory leader said: "It is clear that parts of our mini-Budget went further and faster than markets were expecting, so the way we are delivering our mission now has to change." Her pledge not to raise corporation tax was a casualty of this announcement.
The crisis deepened as Tory MPs finally had enough. Backbencher Robert Halfon went on TV and described ministers as "libertarian jihadists", and within hours the first MP, Crispin Blunt, had publicly called for her to go. Two more, Andrew Bridgen and Jamie Wallis, swiftly followed.
The latter wrote: "Your decision to appoint historical supporters of you personally rather than the most qualified politicians available in the party has led to decisions that have done clear and obvious harm to the British economy." In the coming days more and more MPs would add their name to the list.
Mr Hunt, who had been locked in crisis talks with Ms Truss at Chequers - the Prime Minister's grace-and-favour home in Buckinghamshire - made a surprise announcement, scrapping nearly all of the tax cuts in the mini-Budget. He also said that the energy price guarantee would be reviewed after six months - a screeching climbdown after Ms Truss taunted Labour after promising it would last two years.
There were plenty of bizarre moments during Ms Truss's brief tenure, but few more strange than when she ducked appearing in the House of Commons to answer a question from Keir Starmer. Instead she sent Penny Mordaunt to face the music, but later bizarrely appeared in the chamber behind her and sat silently.
Barraged by questions on October 17, Ms Mourdaunt was forced to insist there "has not been a coup" adding: "The Prime Minister is not under a desk."
Mr Shapps, speaking to an audience in London that night, claimed that Ms Truss was on a knife-edge, saying: "She needs to thread the eye of a needle with the lights off, it's that difficult." His scepticism didn't stand in the way of him accepting the Home Secretary post just two days later. That happened following Suella Braverman's sacking - more on that below.
The public could have been forgiven for thinking Ms Truss's term in charge couldn't get any more chaotic. They were wrong. Suella Braverman was sacked for sending government information from a personal email address.
And problems mounted when Ms Braverman was given the boot. In a scathing letter the shamed cabinet member, who would get her job back less than a week later when Mr Sunak became PM, wrote she had "concerns" about the direction of the government and accused Ms Truss of breaking "key pledges".
It didn't help that one of Ms Truss's most senior advisors, Jason Stein, was suspended amid claims that Number 10 officials had branded Sajid Javid "s***" to a journalist. The PM's press secretary told reporters: "The Prime Minister has made very clear to her team that some of the sort of briefings we have seen are completely unacceptable about parliamentary colleagues and they must stop".
Things got even worse after a spectacular breakdown in discipline during a vote on a Labour motion on fracking, which saw tempers fray and allegations of manhandling. Deputy chief whip Craig Whittacker even reportedly fumed: "I don't give a f*** anymore."
Tories were told that anyone who did not support the Government would have the party whip withdrawn - but 36 MPs failed to vote, although it is unclear how many were rebelling. In a clip that later went viral, backbencher Charles Walker lashed out at "talentless" cabinet members, branding it a "shambles and a disgrace".
After a meeting with Sir Graham Brady, who chaired the influential 1922 committee, Ms Truss finally accepted the inevitable on October 20. She stood at her distinctive jenga-style podium and admitted: "I recognise given the situation I can't deliver the mandate on which I was elected by the Conservative Party." In extraordinary scenes, she said would stay on in No10 until a successor is chosen via a leadership election to be held within the next week.
Ms Truss's resignation smashed the record of the shortest-serving Prime Minister George Canning, who died in office after just 119 days.
